70.s: Walter Johnson never wilted a collar and still looked the same in his seventies.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists

259.t: Playing with Clarence Williams, and drummer Mike Murray

I could play manolene a little bit. The amount that I learned good when I used to play with Clarence Williams,…

259.t: Drummers Hard Yard and Cliff Jones

He went out there to California too. You there yet? He said, I don't know, I heard from him. He said, what did you see there? He said,…

259.s: Vincent recalls violinist Joe Welch and playing with Duck Ernest, whose band included drummer George Evans.

But when he worked to Lewis the man he had a son named Joe. Remember this Joe? I said what Joe's last name is. He just thought about his son. He was a little…

251.t: Drummers Fats Martin and Freddie Coleman
251.s: Albert compares Freddie Coleman to Fats Martin, whom he thought the greatest.

251.s: Interviewer reads a list of Texas musicians; Albert mostly did not know them, remembers drummer Baby Lewis.
251.q: No, Baby Lewis, well I remember him, but that's after he got out of this deal, I saw Baby Lewis in Dallas. He was a good drummer.

105.t: The leading drummers in LA when he was a kid

769.s: He lists Cottrell, Bebe Matthews, Baby Dodds, Henry Martin, Red Happy and Black Benny, plus Two Bits and Cook Shop Son.

288.t: Drum styles, Red Happy, Bebe Matthews and Silver Leaf personnel
288.s: Charles describes Carter's and Red Happy's drumming and the substitute drummers and banjoists of the Silver Leaf band.

634.s: He mentions Woody Williams and Zutty Singleton's uncle, then praises Black Benny as a trap and bass drum player with perfect time who stayed with the band.

634.q: That's how I'm going to play a snare drum. I used to sing when I was a boy. I used to second line. And I always just said I wanted to play a small drum in the brass band. And I adopted his style. And I adopted how he wascapped and walked. And I'd do the same thing.

829.s: Asked about old drummers, Robertson says he knew Manetta, only heard of Walter Brundy, and describes Bolegs from Donaldsonville, who married Claiborne Williams' daughter.

I used to go to a club that used to call the Black Gold in a club that called Chiney Town where he would…

642.s: Trepagnier was a fine timekeeper and master of parade drumming, playing bass drum on parade.
642.q: No finer drummer in the city than him at no time. A fine fellow and a fine musician at all times. Jovial, laughing all the time, and one of the finest timekeepers you ever sat next to. Yeah, yeah.

5.s: Mitchell remembers Hilaire as a good, reading drummer from Louisiana who has since died.
5.ch: Jelly Roll Morton and other records
5.q: Yes, he died. And he was a very good drummer. And he's a good musician too. He could read. He could read. He could read. And he had that, uh, had a good rhythm too. Yeah, sounds fine on him. Yes, Hilaire was good. Hilaire was good. But, uh, I don't think he, uh, got around. But no, I don't think…

925.t: Other good drummers and closing announcement
925.s: Asked about drummers besides Vic Berton, Jernberg names Herb Quigley; the announcer closes the excerpt.
925.q: Well, there were other good drummers. Herb Quigley, for instance.

127.t: Drummers: Red Happy Bolton and Mac Murray
127.s: Punch recalls drummer Happy Goldston, whom he saw at the Regal Theater but never played with; Allen asks about Mac Murray.
127.q: Goldston, yeah. Now, really happy. He was a real good drummer and everything, but I never did play with him. You know, I seen him at the Regal Theater there with Robichoke Bay. I thought he was a mighty good drummer. I thought he was a very good drummer. I thought he was a very good drummer.

881.t: New Orleans drummers: Henry Zeno, Red Happy, Tubby and Minor Hall
881.s: Jackson recalls Henry Zeno's solos, Red Happy as the greatest drummer for execution, the Hall brothers, and the La Rocca boys' neighbourhood.
881.q: And Celestan, Celestan has always read music. Guy Kelly made read music. I know so many fellas that read music. He can't tell me that they didn't read music. And so as I was foreseeing about Celestan, that was a band I really enjoyed. The drums, the drummer, Henry Zeno, used to take a solo, or…

291.t: Oldest-style drummers: Cali Piggott and Dave Bailey
291.s: Barnes names Cali Piggott as the most traditional drummer, then the talk turns to Dave Bailey, whom he does not remember.
291.q: Well, probably he played more than traditional jazz. I don't remember playing with him. In fact, I don't remember him. But, Duck Arnie's brother.

51.t: Joe Lindsey and Henry Martin as drummers
51.s: Ory praises Henry Martin's timekeeping and sound effects, and explains why he was not brought to California.
51.q: He was working in Storoville quite a while with Manuel Perez. He worked with me when, you know, he was on there one night, you see.

689.t: Drummer Norm Downs and Baby Dodds
689.s: Dominique praises Baby Dodds and tells how Baby introduced him to the drummer Norm Downs, who impressed him at a dance and show.
689.q: He didn't care about nobody. George Wettling. George Wettling tried to play like me. Dave Teuf tried to play like me. But there's only one drummer I let come on the bandstand to play. That was Downward.

484.s: Leo Adde as a fine drummer and reader, and Von Gammon's long engagement at the Grand Hotel.
484.q: Leo Addy was one of the finest drummers one of the finest yes Leo Addy was just wonderful fine fine person and very funny man we used to have a lot of fun with him but you know Leo was really a fine reader I don't know whether uh many of you know that but Leo Addy could play in any pit he could…

53.t: Drummers: Baby Dodds, the Happys, Black Benny and Two Bits
53.s: Billy lists the drummers: Baby Dodds, two men named Happy, Two Bits, Ray Dugas, Little Mac and Black Benny. Mary says Benny traveled only with Mac and played a full set; Allen adds details about Bunk Johnson, who worked with them once in Houston.
53.q: Then the drummers that we had from time to time was Baby Dots and a boy named Happy. Yeah, I never did know any other names.

55.t: Opening: early drummer years and bands, 1915 on
55.s: Bill introduces himself, says Alphonse Picou advised him to switch to trombone, and lists the bands he drummed with from 1915.
55.q: Bill Matthews, as old man Bill Matthews speaking, one of the New Orleans original who has been playing jazz for over 40 years, is still going strong, 1959. Born of New Orleans original drummers, 1915 to 1919, it was Alphonse P. Q. Suggestions, you were a young man Billy, my boy, why don't you learn…

831.s: Emmett Hardy was top trumpeter; he also names other trumpeters and good Dixieland drummers like Buck Rogers and Monk Hazel.
831.ch: Early bands and New Orleans musicians
831.q: Well, Tony Majada played fairly good trumpet. He played pretty good trumpet. Dan Hughes played pretty good trumpet. Pete Dickens played pretty good trumpet.

644.t: Pete Masarini, the drummer with no fingers, and his band
644.s: He recalls drummer Pete Masarini, who played with finger stumps, and others in that band including Joe Pelletti, Joe Holbin and a clarinetist around 1912-13.
644.q: You were talking about this drummer without fingers? Yeah, Pete Masarini. He played drums and he had his fingers with all little nubs. The way he used to hold them would get a kick out. Yeah, he was good huh? Yeah, Pete Masarini. He was a joke.

293.t: Sam Hopkins, the Toyamas, Antoines and picnic jobs
293.s: Interviewers ask for contact details of Sam Hopkins, Lawrence Eddergren and the Japanese banjoist; he talks about drummers Paul and Harold Antoine and picnic work.
293.ch: Banjo, piano and his own bands
293.q: Yeah, sure. I got his phone number, his address. I'll give it to you before you go. Okay, yeah. I got them all in my book. Yeah. I got them all, man. All the musicians, you know a lot of them. I got them all in my book. I had Lawrence's. You know Lawrence the piano player? Lawrence, yeah. You know…

1052.t: The Workshop's fruit: John Vodakovich on drums and the group Trinity
1052.s: Without David Lee he struggled to find a drummer and used John Vodakovich, despite criticism, later playing with David Lee and James Singleton in Trinity.
1052.q: It bore many, many beautiful fruit. One of the things that I remember with the absence of David Lee, one of the things I remember with the absence of David Lee, it was very, very frustrating to try to find a drummer that could even play the concept. And when I began to form jazz groups later, one…

56.t: Drummers: Ben Borders and Henry Martin
56.s: Ory rates his drummers and calls Henry Martin a metronome.
56.q: I'm a bop style drummer you know. Oh yeah? Didn't have much beat on the bass drum. Who do you think is the best drummer that you ever played with? You ever had my band? Yeah. Henry Martin. Henry Martin. And the next Ed Robinson boy started out with him. Might have to pull a straw between the two of…

638.t: Early New Orleans drummers he watched or knew
638.s: He names early drummers including Sam Allen, Red Happy, Contrell, Clave, Zeno and Royal of Sam Morgan's band.
638.q: Oh, I used to watch old man Allen had a brother. He called Sam. Sam Allen, I think his name. He was a drummer. But he was a street drummer. He wasn't no St. Allen drummer. Well, drummers I knowed. I knowed Happy. Oh, yeah.

909.t: Outstanding drummers of the old days
909.s: Morris names Happy Goldstein, Bill Norton, Arthur Oglin and Sammy Penn as outstanding drummers.
909.q: No. Black Happy. Black Happy. Happy Goldstein. Happy Goldstein. That's right. Mr. Bill Norton. Now, he's an outstanding drummer. Arthur Oglin, that's an outstanding drummer. Them good drummers.

766.t: Favorite drummers: Cottrell and Piron's band
766.s: He admired old man Cottrell with Piron's band as the king of drummers, and Paul Barbarin.
766.q: He was with P. Rohn. P. Rohn. That's one of the best drumming head, you know, in fact, I mean, he's one of the best. And I see Paul Barbera, I mean, he was good at that time too.

801.s: Eddie names Josiah Frazier; the interviewer took a few drum lessons from him. Eddie calls him among the best drummers, with Louis Barbarin.
801.q: Yeah, when I was little. Well, he's about the best one out there now. Uh-huh. Him and Barberman, Louie Barberman. Uh-huh. And all the two real old ones, Louie and Josiah. They are drummers.

967.t: Big Chief, the Mardi Gras Indians and Professor Longhair's Latin feel
967.s: King plays Big Chief and talks about the tambourine, Mardi Gras Indian songs, Professor Longhair and drummer Charlie Williams.
967.ch: Songwriting and the future of New Orleans music
967.q: They made the tambourine thing become pronounced in music production, doing that kind of thing. And this inspired many people to write compositions around the folk of the Mardi Gras Indians. And the Mardi Gras Indians are the things that you saw. Like Mark Roberts, Ico, Ico. Sure. Ico. Ico. Ico.…

858.t: Good drummers working and in the old days
858.s: Naming good drummers currently and in the old days, ending with the good ones having died.
858.q: You know? Well, George Williams was his name. Yeah. Well, he's not there anymore? I think he's out. I don't think he's out. I don't think he's out. Maybe he's still out. George Williams. You know, Bill Matthews opened up. Yeah.

198.t: Gut-bucket clarinet and the drummers he worked with
198.s: Barnes says he drove bands to play, names drummers such as Black Happy and Dave Bailey, and praises Dave's lively drumming.
198.q: Well really I don't think I could answer you on that. Because my playing was partly different, as I first said. You see I wouldn't play one way. Contour band, this is what I thought that band was playing, and it was fitting that it was coming out right, that's where I went.

715.t: New Orleans trumpeters and Floyd Casey
715.s: Allen recalls Kid Punch and other New Orleans players and his drummer Floyd Casey.
715.q: There was a trumpet player that I had called Kid Punch. I don't know how to grow him. I knew a very bunch of musicians that I had forgotten. And then Kid, it seemed like the old name, Kid something. I had forgotten. I used to hang out with a bunch of them. I don't remember now, it's been so many…

300.t: Comparing a drummer with Walter Brundy and Red Happy
300.s: Allen and Humphrey rate an unnamed drummer-violinist against Walter Brundy and Red Happy.
300.q: Yeah, because on the reading ability. That's a boy named that. He played violin nice. He played nice drum.

58.t: Drummers: Red Happy, Black Benny, Henry Martin
58.q: Them times? Mm-hmm. I'll tell you. Henry Martin was one of the best. Mm-hmm. Well, Happy, I don't believe I've never seen him play. Yeah, I did see him play parade. He played parade with us once. Long time ago. He played nice. I had Black Benny on the bass drum. He's the bad man on the bass drum.…

825.t: Dejan pays a young drummer's union dues: Earl Palmer
825.s: Dejan paid a young drummer's way into the union for a job, and he grew into a top drummer now working in Hollywood. He played with Paul Gayten's group.
825.q: Just to show you how, at that time, they had a young kid that was learning how to play the drums. And he wasn't quite in the union. Harold took money out of his pocket and paid to put him in the union to play that job with him. And it turned out to be one of the best drummers, modern drum players…

574.s: Russell asks about Cookshop Son, his stepfather Jesse and the Silver Leaf band; confusion with Fu Klo and Happy drummers.
574.q: Is he still around? Yeah. If it's the same cook, cause that's the only cookshop son I know. That's what we used to call him. I didn't know he was still living. Did you mean happy? No, I don't think it would be happy.

833.t: Baby Dodds's early drumming and LaRocca again
833.s: He says Baby Dodds played with Buddy Petey and recalls LaRocca living on Third Street.
833.q: I don't know, I believe he was playing then. Go walking and play with him. Buddy Petey. Oh yes, I never knew him but I knew his stepfather but I never knew Buddy. That's who he used to play with. All them old players, like the other boys, I don't know much of them. Yeah, this La Rocca used to live…

194.t: Drummers and New Orleans musicians he knows
194.s: He names Earl Palmer and other drummers, Roy Brown, Sugar Boy, Eddie Bo and Johnny Adams, and says he knows practically every musician in town.
194.ch: Piano influences and the New Orleans scene
194.q: I met a bunch of studs from up there. I just can't call their names cause they wasn't popular, you know what I mean, but they could play but they never was on nothing. You know, there's fill-in men, call them out to sit in on sessions and things like that. Well, it ain't hauling nobody here, Sugar…

311.t: Favorite drummers: Krupa, Buddy Rich, Sam Woodyard, Jo Jones
311.s: He names Gene Krupa, Buddy Rich, Sam Woodyard and Papa Jo Jones as favorites; Clark Terry praised Woodyard.
311.q: Well my favorite drummers I guess, well naturally one of the old ones was Gene Krupa naturally. Buddy Rich was a good friend of mine. And oh gee, what’s the guy, he played with Dizzy Gillespie, what’s his name? Oh Jesus there were several of them.

850.t: Tune In, and Ed Blackwell playing without reading
850.s: Audio excerpt from a Milestone album; Berger describes Blackwell, who never read music yet played every take differently, and compares Han Bennink.
850.ch: Free jazz, time and the Creative Music Studio
850.q: Yeah, this is a tune called “Tune In.” So everybody has the melody. And Blackwell plays with his eyes closed so he doesn’t need any music.

728.t: Bernard Purdie and Bobby Durham lifting the band
728.s: Blue praises drummers Bernard Purdie and Bobby Durham, who elevate a band, including Durham sitting in at Le Duc des Lombards in Paris.
728.q: Purdie. Yes. Yeah Purdie’s a master man. You know it’s as simple as that. He’s strong, he’s determined, he knows music and he knows what he’s looking for in his sound and he knows how to make it work. When Purdie plays the band elevates. You know? There are a few drummers that I’ll say yeah there…

1034.t: Tom Scott's New York Connection and Steve Gadd
1034.s: They sort out Tom Scott's album drummer as Steve Gadd and talk about his Grammy and hi-hat lick.
1034.q: Tom Scott did an album there, it was the LA Express of course. They did the Joni Mitchell stuff. But then he went to New York and did one called the New York Connection with all those guys.

559.t: Dividing guitar parts with Kenny Burrell; egos and Bernard Purdie
559.s: He was the chic guy and Burrell the rhythm guy; egos were not a problem, and he describes Bernard Purdie's signs.
559.q: There were egos but not in the sense that your question is saying. You do this part because I can do it better, it was never anything like that. And if I was playing something the other musicians — I’m not saying Kenny wasn’t always on it, sometimes I was the

580.t: Three drummers with Bill Evans: Motian, Bunker and Arnie Wise
580.s: Israels compares Paul Motian, Larry Bunker and Arnie Wise, and recounts how Wise replaced Bunker after Joe Chambers was passed over.
580.q: I don’t think so. The first drummer was Paul Motian, who did a good job. I wasn’t completely enamored of his playing but I liked it. You know I didn’t find it very — I didn’t find it very beautiful, just the way he hit the drums. His sound. He was a kind of a vertical drummer. But it was okay and I…

337.s: He praises Jake Hanna and Frank Dunlop, remembers June Bug, and cannot tell drummers to swing.
337.q: Yeah. We did a few albums together. He was on the album for Woody Herman in 1964. My favorite, one of my favorite drummers. He just sat back there and swung you know.

498.t: Polyrhythm and drum features in 'In Whom'
498.s: Discussing a Tiny Desk performance, he explains how drummers like Dafnis Prieto and Zachary O'Farrill hear in multiple meters, an African approach, and compares Tony Williams.
498.ch: Rhythm and the African roots of jazz
498.q: Oh you know it’s funny I — sometimes what I do with that section instead of playing those exact notes we’ll play random pitches [scats] and I mean it’s one of those things where really great drummers in this field, people like Dafnis Prieto or my son Zachary O’Farrill, are able to think in…

215.t: Panama Francis, rock and roll stigma, and Bernard Purdie
215.s: Bucky discusses jazz players' disdain for rock and roll drummers, praises Panama Francis and Pretty Purdie, and recalls hearing Purdie on a ship.
215.ch: Studio work in the rock and roll era
215.q: Well he was making good money but he was a good drummer. You take a guy like Pretty [Bernard] Purdie, he was a good drummer no matter where he was: rock & roll or swing, he could do everything.

469.t: Drummer influences: Philly Joe, Blakey, Clarke, Higgins, Buddy Rich
469.s: His biggest drum influences and a Buddy Rich story via Frank DeVito.
469.q: Oh man, well Philly Joe really and “Billy Boy” man, you know, listen to that one. What’s wrong with that? “Billy Boy” man. And Art Blakey man, in the very beginning Art Blakey was just thundering. And Kenny Clarke man. Brushes? Kenny Clarke, what a player man. I loved Billy Higgins though too.…

494.s: Waits's energy, his Motown studio past, his son Nasheed, and his compositions.
494.ch: Recordings as a leader and the Getz years
494.q: Freddie was – he was definitely one of my favorite drummers, and one of my favorite people. We first started playing together with Freddie, Freddie Hubbard. It was he and Herbie Lewis. That was the rhythm section. We just had such a ball, always. Freddie was always so open to different kinds of…

85.s: Interview resumes on Carter's eighty-fifth birthday; he praises Catlett as a gentle giant and wishes today's drummers had heard him.
85.q: Well, what attracted me was his style of drumming, which I certainly cannot analyze here. This is the sort of thing that I always say . . . I use the term ineffable, you know. I think it’s got to be heard and felt. But he was a fine drummer and a lot of people, you know, later drummers, have tried…

703.t: Billy Higgins's ruffs and Herbie Lewis on his albums
703.s: Billy Higgins's ruffs made Sidewinder work; Herbie Lewis plays on Stick Up and Solo/Quartet.
703.q: ruff. “What the heck are you doing, Billy?” Plays ruff ruff ruff. That’s of the secrets of how that Sidewinder – Lee Morgan Sidewinder – worked so good, because Billy could play those ruffs. Ruff ruff ruff. I said, “Man, what are you doing, starting a car or something? What the hell?” He would do…

133.t: Billy Higgins: the instant-fire drummer for a trio
133.s: Walton says Higgins was on fire from the downbeat with no buildup, the ideal trio drummer, with Willie Jones sharing the trait.
133.q: Well, I, I, uh, it's a case of not necessarily looking for something, but knowing it when you see it, when you hear it. Higgins, for instance, is a drummer who, when it's time for the downbeat, he's on fire immediately. There is no buildup. There was no buildup with Higgins. He was on fire, his ear…

504.s: He admires Purdie's reading and grooves.
504.q: Yeah, it was Bernard’s album. We both played drums on it, there are some horn players on it. We play some trades… For me… “Pretty Boy” Purdie is bad, man! He’s a good reader, he can play with big bands, I’ve seen him play with orchestras and he reads really well. He was doing some CTI sessions and…

143.s: He found Muhammad in New Orleans and credits his drumming for the hit sound.
143.q: No-no. I saw him down in New Orleans, and I got him from there. He was down there. I got him from down there. He’s a great drummer. Great beat.

527.t: Kenny Clarke's character and sense of the beat
527.s: Clarke was tasteful, generous and kept the beat on top without rushing.
527.q: Kenny was a very great person. Personally, he was a man. He had lived. He had experience, and he never did anything that was not done in good taste. He didn’t overdo anything. He didn’t make any hassles with nobody. It was not like, “I’m Kenny Clarke,” nothing like that. He was a good model,…

371.t: Kenny Clarke and Shadow Wilson as drummers
371.s: Jones worked at Minton's with Shadow Wilson and praises Kenny Clarke's light touch and brush mastery.
371.ch: 1950s clubs, Savoy dates and the Detroit sound
371.q: No. I worked with Shadow Wilson at a place up… It was at Mittens. Do you remember Mittens? Mittens head sort of gone down from its previous level but they were still doing things there. I worked there with a group with Jerome Richardson, Wendell Marshall, and Shadow Wilson. It was a good group. I…

471.t: Little Harlem drummers Streamline and Al Dunn
471.s: Brower asks about Washington drummers; Cobb describes Streamline and Al "Gotta Be" Dunn.
471.ch: Bostic, Washington clubs and arriving in New York
471.q: Streamline, yeah. Streamline was a guy that stammered. He couldn’t get one word out for maybe five minutes, but he could sing “The green grass grows all around, the green grass grows all around” and not miss a beat. I never could understand that. He used to have to sit up there and sing. When he’d…

460.t: Bernard Purdie and his Hitmaker placards
460.s: Brown and Laws discuss whether Bernard Purdie played on the session and Laws recalls Purdie's habit of posting Hitmaker signs in studios.
460.ch: The Met orchestra and joining CTI
460.q: I can talk to him, because I got his number.

493.t: Meeting Elvin Jones and Max Roach
493.s: He met Elvin Jones and later heard Max Roach play solo at Jazz Fest, where Roach complimented his set.
493.q: him play live?” “No.” “Oh, you got to hear him play live.” “I know. You’re right. I know. This is why I’m looking forward to this day.” I eventually did meet him. I was very honored. I wouldn’t say scared, but I was just really honored, really happy, like, “I’m so glad to finally meet you after all…

228.t: Roy Haynes replaces Tony and favorite drummers
228.s: McLean praises Haynes as in Tony's roots and lists Carvin, Burrage, Eric McPherson, Nasheet Waits and Louis Nash.
228.ch: Later Blue Note years and ending the habit
228.q: Roy is so great. Roy Haynes is like at the seed somewhere. He’s in there in Tony’s roots somewhere. Tony’s roots go down, and you find Roy Haynes under there in the soil.

400.t: Zutty Singleton's $5 favor from Cab and Hinton's love for him
400.s: When Zutty asked Cab for help in New York he got $5; Hinton tells how he loved Zutty, and Taylor praises drummers' personal sounds and Hinton's adaptable bass.
400.ch: Cotton Club, Zutty and Chicago traditions
400.q: So he comes out to the Cotton Club. He comes back stage to Cab. “I just got in town and things ain‟t working too good for me”. He says, “You told me if I ever needed any help… would you help me”? So Cab says, “Oh, yeah, wait a minute, I‟ll be right back. So Cab goes in his dressing room, comes back…

506.t: Drummers Billy Cobham and Harvey Mason
506.s: He praises both drummers for recorded drum sound and their playing.
506.q: Boy, you got some great drums on that list. Billy and I go way back to his first CTI dates. Again, Billy knows how to record the drums. He knows how to get the engineer to record the drums. And he's trying to use a smaller set which is great for me because there's too much shit on the stage. And he…

123.s: He lists drummers who played for him, including Sid Catlett, Bellson, Philly Joe Jones, and Dave Tough, and discusses Stan Levey.
123.q: Yep. And I was fortunate to see a lot of the great ones like Big Sid Catlett... Louis Bellson played for us a lot, and even the character Buddy Rich played for us and played great.

136.t: Eddie Marshall and Gene Cherico as her rhythm section
136.s: How Eddie Marshall joined, the first Japan trip, and his hallmark of a beautiful beat and soft stick touch.
136.ch: New York clubs, marriage and tours
136.q: No, the time when we had a quartet together, Jake was already, he‟d left school—I think he was playing with Woody‟s band—it could be, I think it was Woody Herman‟s band. It could be Maynard‟s [Ferguson], I‟m not quite sure about that part. But, so, Gene Cherico, always he had a knack for finding a…

109.t: Dave Tough: friend and model of accompaniment
109.s: Clarke recalls his closeness to Dave Tough and Casey on 52nd Street and in Chicago, and admired Tough's steady, supportive drumming over Buddy Rich's rushing.
109.ch: Minton's, Louis Armstrong and the South
109.q: Oh, I loved them. Davey. He would say, 'That's wonderful, Kenny.' 'That was really wonderful.' You know, he would talk like that. Then he joined -- what was that trumpet player's band? He was in Chicago.

26.t: Admired drummers and how he developed his own style
26.s: Greer praises Zutty, Baby Dodds, Catlett, Chick Webb and Kaiser Marshall, then says his style came from intuition, watching the Capitol Theatre drummer and the soloist's left hand; brushes at Gregory's.
26.ch: The Washingtonians, Bechet and drum style
26.q: Zutty, well, Zutty was one of my best pals. Good drummer. Baby, good drummer. Good drummer. beautiful drummer. Sidney Catlett, /Chick Webb, beautiful drumer. Kaiser was a beautiful drummer. He fitted Fletcher's band like a glove. He used to tell everybody he was my brother.

4.s: Sonny Clay drummed in Johnny's band before leading his own band to Australia.
4.ch: Publishing, Jelly Roll in Los Angeles and band lore
4.q: Well, Sonny Clay, he was a drummer, you know, and he played a little piano, too. And he had his own band after a while. He played piano in his own band. When he played with my brother... See, my brother had a...I told you he had...he had a band that...of...of musicians, and Sonny was the drummer in…

9.s: James was a Chick Webb bassist; Spencer was young and wild drummer of the Blue Rhythm Band.
9.q: Oh, that's my boy. O'Neil Spencer. I don't know when and how I met him, or where. It was in somebody's band. I don't know if it was... I don't know how you can work with people and don't know when was the first time you saw them or anything. Yeah, I knew Spencer very well. He was with the Blue…

106.t: Bechet leaves with Benny Peyton; Buddy Gilmore
106.s: Bechet joined Benny Peyton's Jazz Kings; Briggs describes Peyton as a schooled percussionist and Buddy Gilmore as a showman drummer who worked with Vernon Castle.
106.ch: Will Marion Cook and the Southern Syncopated Orchestra
106.q: No, no, he didn't stay with Lattimore. Bechet had gotten out with Benny Peyton's group, Benny Peyton formed the Jazz Kings and --

379.s: He heard of a heavy-percussion band and doubts Cozy's style fit.
379.q: to see it. He invite me a couple times for rehearsals, something like that. He was doing something by Gene Krupa.

90.s: On a break he hears Sid Catlett with Allan Eager's quartet.
90.ch: Wartime South and the Ernie Fields band
90.q: In fact, that's where I first heard the great Sid Catlett. While we were playing at the Club Alabam, we were playing for the big production and we were doing our thing. Melvin White... We also had another fine singer named Estelle Edmonson(?) with the band. And on my break, I walked down to the…

758.s: Roy talks about Zutty's moods and habit of dropping the volume.
758.q: : I really don't know. I mean, he had problems with Louis, too, you know. I just really could never figure him out, you know. He always thought somebody was plotting against him or something. Like he would tell me, he said 'You ought to watch the trumpet ...(?)..., because they got black hearts' --…

383.t: Drummers of the thirties: Kaiser Marshall, Walter Johnson and Big Sid
383.s: Wilson praises Walter Johnson's open top cymbal, Jo Jones's change of style, and Big Sid's ageless playing.
383.q: very fond of Kaiser's drumming. I heard him with Fletcher Henderson's band years before in Detroit, before we came to New York. And I liked also, very much, Walter Johnson. Walter Johnson was the best drummer I heard playing an open-top cymbal, big cymbal on top of the drum and just letting it ring…

93.t: Drummers as blood brothers and other dancers of the day
93.s: Green says tap dancer and drummer are blood brothers, and lists Roland James, Baby Lawrence, Groundhog, Taps Miller and novelty dancers like George Rochette.
93.q: Well, they were what they call blood brothers, because the drummer played the rhythm for the music of the band, and the tap dancer is all rhythm, see. So, it's as simple as that. That's the relation to the drummer, you see. Like, you had the tempo by the drums, you see.

566.t: Drummers: Ed Thigpen, Jo Jones and Cozy Cole
566.s: Ed Thigpen went abroad with Humes and lives in Europe, and his father was a good drummer. Humes calls Jo Jones her alma mater, and Cozy Cole sweet and reliable.
566.q: He was one of the great ones.

29.t: Drummers, pianists and guitarists he remembers
29.s: Howard cannot recall many good drummers, praises Sonny Clay and Charlie Lawrence on piano, and knows no good guitarists.
29.ch: Reel 2: Los Angeles musicians, the Apex and Cotton Club
29.q: No. You had to be good to leave an impression on me, because I'm hard -- You're hard to please.

72.s: Moore and Dodds drank and talked drums; Dodds had his own style with rim work and press rolls and little cymbal.

412.t: Sidney Bechet scolds a drummer on playing a chorus
412.s: Hodes describes Bechet berating a drummer who took a full chorus and shortened it. He and DeMichael discuss how drummers took breaks and mention Sid Catlett.
412.ch: Jam sessions, pay and the Vanguard (retyped)
412.q: Stand in line, just to sit in. And let me tell you something about drummers that you might be surprised to hear. We have a fellow by the name of Kansas around Chicago. And he supposedly was a tremendous drummer. Now, in those days, like I say, drums was not breaking it up and all that nonsense. And…

388.t: Ray McKinley's sound and a short job in his band
388.s: Leeman admires McKinley's tuning and swing and recalls joining his band for five or six weeks.
388.q: I mention Ray McKinley, a great drummer, whom I heard with the Dorsey brothers around '32 or '33. I heard him a couple of times in person on one nighters, and in Massachusetts and then back in my home town on the radio from Glen Island Casino -- I loved the sound of his drums, Ray McKinley. 74.t: Trent takes over the band and A.G. Godley joins
74.s: Trent becomes leader, brings in Joe Haymen and Swazey, replaces his cousin on drums with A.G., and they play a summer resort in Muskogee.
74.ch: Trent's band: Arkansas, Dallas and the Adolphus
74.q: Yeah. -------- took over the band and he got Joe Haymen, Swazey and I said his cousin was on drums and he heard A.G. A.G. came down, we went to Muskogee and played in a place called Stem Beach.

76.t: Baby Dodds and Red Happy's drum contest
76.s: Zutty knew Baby Dodds in New Orleans; Dodds and Red Happy had a drumming contest on Zutty's drums, and a Preservation Hall drummer says he learned from Red Happy.
76.ch: New Orleans bands, Louis and the Lyric
76.q: Why sure, sure. Him and (Red Happy?) had a contest on my drums.

238.t: Sid Catlett as friend and melodic drummer
238.s: Sid Catlett played on one of her record sessions and she admires his melodic, listenable drumming.
238.q: Oh, yes, he played at my house. In fact he did one record with me, record session. He did -- I can't remember all of the things. What else did we do on that? We did, "The Song is Ended, But the Melody Lingers On." He was on that session with me. Also, Irving Ashby, the guitarist, second guitarist…

78.t: Big Sid Catlett's drumming in Fletcher's rhythm section
78.s: Catlett took charge, set Fletcher's tempos, fed soloists and could be heard in four-bar solos without overpowering the band.
78.ch: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
78.q: Big Syd Catlett. Yes, I had the pleasure of being in the rhythm section with him in Fletcher's band. And this happened in the Grand Terrace days too, the "Christopher Columbus" era, along with Chu Berry and Roy. Big Syd was a great fellow. He was a take-charge type of fellow,

171.t: Sid Catlett, Kenny Clarke and how a rhythm section builds choruses
171.s: Sid Catlett was the boss; Ramey worked with him from 1946 and explains the second-chorus lift.
171.q: Sidney Catlett was the boss. He was the boss, and we finally started working together in '46 down on 52nd Street, and I got, oh, placards and billboards of advertisements of many jobs that we had together, you know, especially on Sunday afternoons, you know, where they had the featured All-Stars,…
